subject: Business
title: Scenario Planning Before the Table
description: A fast breakdown of Scenario Planning Before the Table for builders.

hook.text: The other side rejects your first offer. Now what? If you didn't plan for this, you're improvising.

buildup.text: Scenario planning means mapping out multiple paths: best case, worst case, and likely case.

discovery.text: For each scenario, prepare a response, a concession you can trade, and a redirection.

twist.text: The other side has prepared too. If their moves surprise you, your preparation was too narrow.

climax.text: Chess grandmasters think five moves ahead. Top negotiators prepare at least three paths forward.

punchline.text: Don't plan your script. Plan your decision tree.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of scenario planning in negotiation?
options: Preparing multiple response paths for different outcomes
Predicting exactly what the other side will say
Writing a script to follow word-for-word

details.summary: Scenario planning maps out multiple possible negotiation paths before sitting at the table, preparing responses for different moves the other side might make.
details.whyItMatters: Negotiators who are surprised by unexpected moves make poor decisions under pressure. Scenario planning eliminates most surprises by pre-computing responses, allowing you to react thoughtfully rather than reflexively when the negotiation takes
takeaways: Map out likely scenarios and your optimal response to each before negotiating
Anticipating the other side's moves prevents surprise-driven poor decisions
Prepare fallback positions for each key issue if your preferred outcome fails

faq.question: How detailed should negotiation scenario planning be?
faq.answer: Plan for three to five likely scenarios including best case, worst case, and most probable. For each scenario, prepare your response and identify the concessions you would make. Define your walk-away point for each path. Over-planning for unlikely scenarios wastes preparation time.

faq.question: How do you scenario plan when you have limited information about the other side?
faq.answer: Use industry benchmarks and public information to estimate their likely positions. Consider their incentives and constraints based on their role and organization. Plan questions that will reveal information early in the negotiation. Adjust your scenarios as you learn more during the process.
